To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the neurons in the inferior colliculi are labelled retrogradely after the injection of [3H]-aspartate into the inferior collicular complex.

the retrograde transport of [3H]- D-aspartate, after injection into the inferior colliculi, is restricted to the dorsal and intermediate nuclei of the lateral lemniscal pathway, the auditory cortex, and a number of nuclei in the reticular and brain stem tegmentum.

the distribution of neurons labelled by the retrograde transport of [3H]-aspartate injected into inferior colliculus of the cat is similar to that of neurons labelled by retrograde transport of horseradish peroxidase injected into the colilculus inferior.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of the neurotransmitter used for the transmission of sound in the auditory system.
the question if the transmission of auditory signals through the inferior collieculus is mediated by the neurotransmitter glutamate or asparate.
a possible transmitter function of the aspartate.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the neurons of the inferior colliculi are mainly labelled by [3H]-d-aspartate and therefore are probably glutamate or asparate neurons.

the inferior colliculi receive their afferents from the lateral and dorsal nuclei of the lateral lemniscus, from the cochlear nuclei, the superior olivary complex, the auditory cortex, the reticular formation, the parabranchial and the raphe nuclei and the lateral hypothalamus.
the inferior colliculi of the cat is not a transmitter for D-aspartate.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
[3H]-aspartate injected into inferior colliculus labels cells in the auditory brainstem and the auditory cortex and also cells in non-auditory brainstem nuclei and in the hypothalamus.
the neurons in the lateral lemniscus, the cochlear nuclei and the auditory cortical neurons are the main candidates for the transmission of the acoustic information.
neurons in the inferior colliculi of cats receive their afferents from the dorsal and intermediate nuclei of the lateral lemniscus and from the cochlear nuclei.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the inferior colliculi of the cat are not the sole target for [3H]D-aspartate in the auditory system.
[3H]-aspartate is a good retrograde marker for neurons projecting to the inferior colliculi.
the inferior colliculi of the cat are not the only auditory structures that contain neurons that are sensitive to D-aspartate.
